entry.title: Detroit's outfield is 3 men down. Here's what that's actually worth, and it's less than it sounds
entry.summary: Greene, Vierling and Carpenter are all on the injured list with Detroit half a game out and 42 to play. Measured against the players actually replacing them, the 3 of them together are worth about 1.5 wins the rest of the way, and 79 percent of that is Greene alone. The catch is Carpenter, who's having the worst year of his career and is probably better than his line says.
entry.content:
Riley Greene went on the 10-day injured list Wednesday with a right hamstring strain. He's got 492 plate appearances and an .816 OPS, easily Detroit's best outfielder, and he joins Matt Vierling and Kerry Carpenter, who are already there. 3 outfielders, on a team that's half a game out of the last wild card spot with 42 to play.

Worth being accurate about how big a bat this is, because I nearly wasn't. Greene is not Detroit's best hitter. Among the 6 guys with 300 or more plate appearances he's 3rd in OPS, behind Dillon Dingler at .844 and Kevin McGonigle at .819, and McGonigle has more plate appearances than he does. Greene's the best outfielder on the roster and the 3rd best hitter, and those are different sentences.

So it reads like the season just ended. I don't think it does, and I want to show you why, including the part that argues the other way.

First, they didn't all go down at once

This matters more than it sounds, because "we just lost 3 outfielders" and "we lost 1 more outfielder having already lost 2" are pretty different sentences.

From the league's own transactions feed:

PlayerPlacedInjuryEligible to return
Kerry CarpenterJul 27Left foot plantar fasciitisAug 6
Matt VierlingJul 31, retro to Jul 30Left adductor strainAug 9
Riley GreeneAug 12Right hamstring strainAug 22

Carpenter's been out 17 days and Vierling 14. Both of them passed their 10-day minimum a while back and neither is back, which is its own small worry, and plantar fasciitis is the kind of thing that lingers. But the point for right now is that Detroit's already been playing shorthanded for 2 weeks. Only 1 of these 3 is new information.

On Greene specifically, A.J. Hinch said the club thinks the strain is mild, and that Greene felt it slowing up at home plate and never hobbled, which Hinch called a good sign as opposed to a big mid-belly grab. A Cody Stavenhagen quote going around r/motorcitykitties has Hinch saying he wouldn't have been able to play the rest of this series or the White Sox weekend anyway, which I'm passing on second hand rather than from the piece itself. Take the 10-day minimum at face value and that's about 9 games.

Second, and this is the part nobody says out loud

Only 1 of the 3 was hitting.

PlayerPAOPSvs replacement (.604)
Riley Greene492.816+.212
Kerry Carpenter259.692+.088
Matt Vierling291.590-.014
Max Clark50.804+.200
Ben Malgeri57.730+.126
James Outman100.606+.002
Corey Julks2.000called up Wednesday

Vierling's at .590. That's below the level of a randomly grabbed bench guy, and I'll show you where that .604 comes from in a second. Carpenter's at .692, which is under the league's .719 and under Detroit's own team mark of .727. Greene is the only one of the 3 who was clearly making the team better by being in the lineup.

The replacement number isn't something I remembered, it's derived. Every non-pitcher in baseball with under 150 plate appearances this season, 267 of them, 15,352 trips to the plate, hits .280/.324 for a .604 OPS. That's the population a club actually reaches for when a regular goes down, and it's exactly the group Detroit's reaching for now. Julks has 2 plate appearances this season, Clark has 50, Malgeri 57, Outman 100. All 4 of them are inside that bucket.

I deliberately did not use Detroit's replacements' own numbers as the baseline, because Max Clark hitting .804 in 50 plate appearances tells you nothing and using it would flatter the argument I'm making. The league-wide bucket is the more conservative choice and it's the one the math below runs on.

So what's it worth in wins

Fit runs per plate appearance on OPS across all 30 teams this season and you get runs/PA = -0.1218 + 0.3340 x OPS, r-squared .830. So 100 points of OPS is worth about .033 runs every time you come up. Detroit's scored 549 and allowed 462 in 120 games, which puts a win at about 10.4 runs.

Give each guy the plate appearances he was taking per game he played, times the games he misses:

ScenarioRunsWins
Greene out all 42 remaining12.51.20
Carpenter out all 424.00.38
Vierling out all 42-0.6-0.06
All 3, rest of season15.81.52
Greene for the 10-day minimum, about 9 games2.70.26

Worst case, all 3 miss every remaining game, it's about a win and a half, and 79 percent of that is Greene. Vierling's line is negative, meaning the numbers say Detroit is very slightly better with him on the shelf, which I'd treat as "costs nothing" rather than as an actual gain.

The realistic case is the bottom row. Greene misses 9 or so, the other 2 come back somewhere in there, and the whole thing costs a quarter of a win.

Now the argument against all of that

Carpenter. His .692 is by a distance the worst season of his career. He went .811, .932 and .788 the 3 years before this one, 1,219 plate appearances that weight out to about .832. Treating a guy's worst 259 plate appearances as his true talent is exactly the error I'd complain about if somebody else did it.

Run him at .832 instead and he's worth 10.2 runs over 42 games rather than 4.0, right about a full win on his own. That takes the 3-man total from 1.52 wins to 2.12 and drops Greene's share from 79 percent to 57. So the honest version of the headline is that 2 of the 3 matter and 1 of them doesn't, not that this is all about Greene.

Small note on that .832, since I'd want to know: it's his 2023 to 2025 seasons weighted by plate appearances, which is an approximation. Doing it properly means rebuilding on-base and slugging from the raw components rather than averaging 3 OPS figures. It'd move the number a little, not enough to change anything here.

Vierling doesn't get the same defence. He was at .717 and .735 in his first 2 Detroit years, then .617 in 100 plate appearances last year, then .590. That's 2 years of going the wrong way, not 1 bad stretch.

A few other things this method can't see, and I'd rather say them than have you find them:

  • OPS knows nothing about defence. Vierling's the center fielder. Handing center to Outman or a rookie is a real cost and none of the arithmetic above can price it. If Vierling's glove is worth half a win out there, most of my "he costs nothing" disappears.
  • A team-level fit used on 1 player pretends to be more precise than it is. That r-squared of .830 is across 30 teams and thousands of plate appearances each. Pointing it at 176 plate appearances from 1 man gives you a number with a decimal point and not really that much behind the decimal point.
  • Greene's rate assumes he plays every game he's available for. He wouldn't have. So 1.20 is a bit high.

What the last 2 weeks actually looked like

Here's the thing I keep going back and forth on. Since Carpenter went down on July 27, Detroit's played 14 games and gone 9-5, scoring 7.43 runs a game. Before that they were at 4.20.

That's a huge number and I don't believe it means much. It's 14 games, and it includes 14-0 and 13-1 and 11-0 and 11-0 again, so a couple of blowouts are carrying most of it. Nobody should walk away thinking the Tigers are better without their outfielders. What it's decent evidence of is the narrower thing: the offence has not fallen over without Carpenter and Vierling, and it had 14 games to.

Where this leaves them

59-61, half a game back of Texas for the last spot and level with Minnesota, 42 to go, with 6 teams inside 2 games of each other. It's about as tight as it gets.

And that's the part that keeps me from filing this under "no big deal." A quarter of a win sounds like nothing, and in a normal August it is nothing. In a race where 6 teams are separated by 2 games, a quarter of a win is a real slice of what's left. The injuries aren't a disaster and the panic version of this story is wrong, but "it's small" and "it doesn't matter" aren't the same claim, and in this race they come apart.

If Greene's back around the 22nd and Carpenter's foot finally settles down, this is a footnote. If the hamstring turns into 6 weeks, the number to be scared of is 1.2 wins, and Detroit doesn't have 1.2 wins to give away.

All figures from the MLB Stats API on August 13, 2026, derived in one run by scripts/tigers_outfield.py. Not betting advice.

Sources: MLB.com on Greene's IL placement · Detroit News

entry.title: Pick No. 5: Nobody runs on either of these guys, and that costs Cleveland more than Detroit
entry.summary: Keider Montero and Parker Messick are 2nd and 3rd of 58 qualified starters at stopping people from even trying to steal. Between them, 3 attempts in 259 innings. Detroit never runs anyway, so the lockdown lands almost entirely on Cleveland. Tigers, Low.
entry.content:
The call: Detroit takes the series finale Thursday afternoon at Comerica. Confidence: low.

Yesterday the question here was whether Detroit should be running on Cleveland. The answer was mostly yes, and the running-game edge in Wednesday night's game actually belonged to Cleveland, because Framber Valdez has let 13 runners steal and thrown out none of them.

Thursday afternoon the same series produces the opposite game entirely. Of the 58 qualified starters in baseball, exactly 1 is harder to run on than either of the 2 men starting this one, and he pitches for Milwaukee.

Nobody runs on these two

Take every qualified starting pitcher in baseball, 58 of them, and count steal attempts allowed per 9 innings. Not stolen bases, and not the rate runners get thrown out, because both of those are mostly a story about the catcher. Attempts is the pitcher's number. It's his time to the plate, his pickoff move, his handedness, and it's the closest free measure of whether a runner even considers it.

Keider Montero is 2nd of 58. Parker Messick is 3rd.

Rank of 58PitcherAttempts allowedInningsPer 9
1Jacob Misiorowski, Milwaukee1133.00.07
2Keider Montero, Detroit1122.10.07
3Parker Messick, Cleveland2136.20.13
4Shota Imanaga, Chicago Cubs3137.10.20
5Michael McGreevy, St. Louis4126.00.29
29, the medianTaj Bradley, Minnesota10131.20.68
38Framber Valdez, Detroit13127.10.92
58Chase Burns, Cincinnati26124.01.89

Between them, Messick and Montero have faced 3 attempted steals in 259 innings. 2 median starters over the same workload would face about 20.

And here's the part I liked most: neither of them has thrown out a single runner. Montero has allowed 1 stolen base and caught nobody. Messick has allowed 2 and caught nobody. This isn't a couple of guys with rocket arms behind them gunning people down. It's that in 259 innings, 3 people have thought it was worth trying.

Which lands almost entirely on Cleveland

Detroit doesn't run. That's been true all year and it was the finding two days ago: 53 attempts in 1,100 times reached first, 4.8%, dead last of 30 teams. So Messick shutting down the Detroit running game is like locking a door nobody uses. Call it 0.4 attempts a game that Detroit wasn't going to make anyway.

Cleveland does run, and does it well. 117 steals, 23 caught, 83.6% success, attempting on 12.7% of times reached first. In a normal game they reach first about 9 times, so that's a bit over 1 attempt a game they'd like to have. Against Montero it's approximately zero.

Now the honest size of that. 1 attempt is not a game. If you handed me a lineup card and told me only that Cleveland's running game was switched off, I would move the number by a fraction of a run and no more. What makes it worth writing about is that Cleveland's offense doesn't have many other tools. They're 28th in baseball in runs scored, and 26th in OPS against right-handed pitching, which is what Montero is. The bases were one of the few places they were above average, and Thursday it's shut.

The rest of the game

Detroit is 59-60 and 2.5 back of the White Sox with the division wide open. They have won 8 of 10 and 3 in a row. Cleveland is 58-62, has lost 8 of 10 and 3 in a row, and is 4 back.

Under the records, the gap is bigger than 1 game in the standings. Detroit has scored 545 runs and allowed 456, and that run prevention number is 3rd best in baseball. Cleveland has scored 477 and allowed 506. That's a Detroit team outscoring its opponents by 89 against a Cleveland team being outscored by 29.

Home team, better team, hotter team, against a lineup that's 26th against righties. That's the call.

What scares me

Messick is the better pitcher and it isn't close. 2.57 ERA over 23 starts, 1.04 WHIP, 136 strikeouts in 136.2 innings. His fielding independent numbers back most of it up: 3.19 FIP, 3.44 xFIP. He is a 25-year-old lefty having a genuinely excellent season and Detroit is exactly league average against left-handed pitching, 15th of 30 at a .706 OPS. That's the whole case for Cleveland and it's a good one.

Montero's numbers are prettier than his pitching. A 1.01 WHIP looks outstanding until you notice he has 86 strikeouts in 122.1 innings, which is about 6.3 per 9, and that his xFIP is 4.57 against a 3.38 ERA. That's a run-and-a-fifth gap between what he's given up and what his strikeouts, walks and flyballs say he should have given up. He also gets hit harder at home, 3.79 at Comerica against 2.77 on the road, so the park isn't the trick either. I went looking for that explanation and it isn't there.

These 2 have already done this once and Cleveland won. May 19 at Comerica, Messick against Montero, Cleveland 4 Detroit 3. Messick went 5 and gave up 2. Montero went 5, gave up 3, and walked 4 while striking out 1.

And the season series is 1-6. Detroit finally beat Cleveland on Monday for the first time in 7 tries. The piece on this site that went looking for the reason concluded there mostly isn't one, and I still believe that. But 1-6 is 1-6, and I'm picking the team that owns the losing end of it.

Not betting advice.

entry.title: Graded: Pick No. 4. The first miss, and the catcher I told you wouldn't be out there caught all 9 innings
entry.summary: The call was Tigers win, Low. Final: Cleveland 6, Detroit 4. I told 2 commenters the running lane they wanted was closed because Patrick Bailey would be catching. Bailey never left the bench. Austin Hedges caught the whole game, Detroit reached 1st base 8 times, and nobody went.
entry.content:
The call, committed before first pitch: Tigers win. Confidence Low.

The result: Cleveland 6, Detroit 4. gamePk 824241, Final on the id.

Record: 3-1.

Detroit falls to 59-61, 3.5 back of the White Sox and half a game out of the last wild card. Cleveland is 7-1 against them this year.

I got the catcher wrong, and it's the part of the entry that mattered

Yesterday's piece answered 2 commenters who wanted Detroit running on Cleveland. I said they were right about Cleveland, right about Detroit, and wrong about the night, for this reason:

So tonight you've got a lefty who runners mostly don't test, and probably the catcher who's been throwing people out. The 5.1% guy is the backup now. The edge you're describing is real and it's aimed at a matchup that isn't on the field tonight.

Austin Hedges caught all 9 innings. Patrick Bailey was on the bench and never came in.

The 5.1% guy, the one who has thrown out 2 runners all season, was on the field the entire time. The matchup the thread was pointing at was exactly the matchup that showed up, and I'm the one who told them it wouldn't.

Worth separating 2 things there, because only 1 of them was wrong. The number was right: Bailey had caught 7 of Cleveland's 9 games in August, Hedges 4, and that checked out then and checks out now at 7 and 5. What was wrong was reading a 10 game sample as a depth chart. Cleveland has alternated all month, and last night was Hedges' turn.

And Detroit still didn't run

8 times on 1st base. Singles plus walks plus hit by pitches, same approximation the original entry used.

0 steal attempts.

Cleveland's pitchers threw over to 1st 6 times, 5 of them by Foster Griffin in the 3rd and 4th. Nobody went.

Here's the part where I have to talk myself down, because this is the number I wanted. Detroit attempts a steal on 4.8% of times reached 1st, and 8 baserunners at 4.8% buys you 0.4 attempts. Zero is the expected result. One game with 8 runners on cannot tell you whether a team ignored an open door or just had a normal night, and if Detroit had gone once I'd have been writing that the door was open and they walked through it, off the same nothing of a sample.

So the honest version is narrow: the specific reason I gave for saying no tonight was wrong, and the game did not produce enough baserunners to test what the readers were actually asking. Thursday afternoon is Parker Messick, who's 3rd of 58 qualified starters at suppressing attempts, so that one won't answer it either.

Cleveland didn't run either, which nobody predicted including me

The entry's other half was that the real running game edge in this game belonged to Cleveland, who attempt on 12.7% and convert 83.6%, against a Framber Valdez who'd allowed 13 steals and caught nobody:

Detroit's catchers are above average, which helps. But the team with the running game edge in this game is Cleveland, going the other direction, and in a 1 run game that's where it'll show up.

Cleveland reached 1st base 13 times and attempted 0 steals.

2 teams, 21 runners on 1st, 0 attempts, in a game between the sport's most aggressive baserunning team by rate and the sport's least. I spent about 2,000 words on the running game and the running game did not occur.

What actually decided it was the walks

Valdez went 5.2 and gave up 4 earned on 6 hits and 5 walks. Detroit's staff walked 7 in total. Cleveland scored 6 on 10 hits and those 7 free passes.

Detroit led 3-2 after 3 innings. Cleveland got 2 in the 5th, 2 more in the 7th off Ty Madden and Enmanuel De Jesus, and that was the game.

The thing I said scared me was Griffin, on the grounds that he's the better pitcher and I was picking the worse one. Griffin went 5 innings and gave up 3 runs, only 1 of them earned, and handed the ball off with a 4-3 lead. He wasn't the problem. The pitcher I defended was, and I defended him by pointing at 2 good starts:

Valdez has a 4.17 ERA which isn't good, but his last 2 starts are 14 innings and 2 earned runs.

That's 2 starts. I knew it was 2 starts when I wrote it.

The pillar held up and then it didn't

The entry's own argument against itself was Cleveland's offense: 28th in baseball at 3.98 runs a game, and 4.00 a game against Detroit specifically over 6 meetings. I called it the pillar that had produced nothing.

They scored 6. That's their 2nd most against Detroit this season, behind an 8 on May 18. Across the 8 games the season series is now Cleveland 34 runs to Detroit's 21, 4.25 a game to 2.62.

I've now written 2 entries arguing that Detroit's 0-6 against Cleveland was variance rather than a mechanism. The permutation test behind that still says what it said. But the record is 1-7, and at some point "it's variance" stops being an analysis and starts being a thing I keep saying.

Sources: MLB Stats API, pulled 2026-08-13, for the final, the box score, the play by play, both pitching lines, the August catcher assignments game by game, the season series and the standings.

He was at 25.0% with the Giants, so some of that is probably the pitchers in front of him and I wouldn't want to give him all the credit. It's still not a guy you run on casually.

And Bailey has caught 7 of Cleveland's 9 games this month, to Hedges' 4, with both appearing in 2. He caught last night. If Cleveland is drifting toward Bailey as the everyday guy, the lane you're all pointing at is closing.

You saw it happen last night, actually. Báez went for 3rd in the 7th, Bailey's throw beat him, and José Ramírez dropped it, and Báez scored. That run came from a Cleveland error, not from a stolen base. The throw was fine.

(Those 3 catcher lines add to 78 steals allowed and the team total is 86. The other 8 are attribution I can't cleanly resolve, so I'm flagging it rather than quietly rounding.)

You're also right that Detroit doesn't run

This part isn't close. Detroit attempts a steal on 4.8% of the times a batter reaches 1st base, and that's dead last in baseball. Houston is next at 4.9%. Miami is at 14.7%, roughly 3 times Detroit's rate.

"Times on 1st" here is singles plus walks plus hit by pitches. It misses reaching on an error and it counts a walk that got erased on the next pitch, so it's an approximation. It's the same approximation for all 30 teams, which is what matters for the comparison.

Here's the counterweight nobody in the thread mentioned though. Detroit is 35 for 53. That's 66.0%. The league runs at 76.9%. So Detroit doesn't just run rarely, they run badly, and the rough break even on a steal is usually put somewhere around 70 to 75%. Telling this team to run more, at the rate they've actually converted, is telling them to give away outs.

That's an argument for running better, not for running less. But it's a real answer to "just go more" and I didn't want to skip past it.

Max Clark, though. He's played 10 games, has 46 plate appearances, and has attempted 0 steals. He made his debut on the road and played his 1st game at Comerica last night. I get the excitement, I've got it too, but there's no evidence either way on him yet and building a strategy around 46 plate appearances is how you end up wrong in public.

The other half of the answer is McKinstry at 1 for 6. That's most of Detroit's caught stealings from one player, and it's probably a chunk of why the staff stopped giving green lights.

And now tonight, which is where I break with you

Foster Griffin gets the ball for Cleveland. He's a lefty. Lefties face 1st base.

Griffin has allowed 6 steals in 133.1 innings and nobody has been thrown out. That's 0.40 attempts per 9 innings, and among the 57 qualified starters in baseball the median is 0.68. He ranks 14th at suppressing the running game. Not elite, top quartile, and enough to trim the opportunity.

So tonight you've got a lefty who runners mostly don't test, and probably the catcher who's been throwing people out. The 5.1% guy is the backup now. The edge you're describing is real and it's aimed at a matchup that isn't on the field tonight.

Thursday might be different. That's Parker Messick, who's 3rd of those same 57 starters at suppressing steal attempts, so honestly, maybe not.

The bigger running game problem tonight is the other one

Cleveland attempts on 12.66% of their times on 1st, and they're 117 for 140, 83.6%. They run constantly and they're good at it.

Framber Valdez has allowed 13 steals and caught nobody, 0.92 attempts per 9, 38th of 57 qualified starters.

Detroit's catchers are above average, which helps. But the team with the running game edge in this game is Cleveland, going the other direction, and in a 1 run game that's where it'll show up.

The call

Tigers win. Low.

Detroit's offense is 11th in baseball at 4.58 runs a game and Cleveland's is 28th at 3.98. Detroit is 8-2 in their last 10 and Cleveland is 2-8. Detroit is home, 59-60, half a game out of the last wild card, and they just scored 6 on a team that had held them to 1.83 a game.

Valdez has a 4.17 ERA which isn't good, but his last 2 starts are 14 innings and 2 earned runs, and the ugly number in his last 6 is one start against the Cubs where he got 2 outs and gave up 6.

What scares me. Griffin is the better pitcher. He's got a 3.31 ERA over 23 starts, 3.06 of it across 22 starts with Washington before the trade, against Valdez at 4.17. I'm picking the worse starter and calling it Low for that reason.

Cleveland is also 6-1 against Detroit this year and the piece I wrote about that concluded there's no mechanism behind it, just variance. Believing my own conclusion means last night was the correction starting. Believing my eyes means Cleveland does something to this lineup that I can't measure. I've written down that it's variance, so I'm picking accordingly, and if they lose 3 of 4 in this series I'll have been wrong twice with the same argument.

entry.title: Graded: Pick No. 3. Detroit beats Cleveland for the first time all year, and the scary pitcher was the one who broke
entry.summary: The call was Tigers win, Low. Final: Detroit 6, Cleveland 4. Drew Anderson faced 17 batters, which is exactly what the entry said would happen, and Tanner Bibee gave up 5 earned runs after coming in with a 1.80 ERA against Detroit.
entry.content:
The call, committed before first pitch: Tigers win. Confidence Low.

The result: Detroit 6, Cleveland 4. gamePk 824240, Final on the id.

Record: 3-0.

That's Detroit's 1st win over Cleveland this season in 7 tries, and it moves them to 59-60, 2.5 back of the White Sox and half a game out of the last wild card spot. They're 8-2 in their last 10.

The Anderson call was right in the boring way, which is the good way

The whole entry rested on 1 number: Drew Anderson had never faced more than 18 batters in a major league game, and Detroit's median start goes 22. The question wasn't whether he'd pitch well, it was how long they'd let him.

He faced 17. 4 innings, 4 hits, 1 earned run, 2 walks, 4 strikeouts, and then Jacob Waguespack for 2 innings. Detroit pulled him a batter short of his career high with a lead, which is the most predictable thing they could've done and it's still nice when the number you built the piece on holds up.

So the bullpen threw 5 innings, which was the actual bet.

Bibee was the thing to be scared of and he's the one who fell over

The other half of the entry was Tanner Bibee, who came in with 15 innings and 3 earned runs against Detroit across 2 starts this year. A 1.80 ERA against a team that couldn't score on anybody in Cleveland's uniform.

He went 6.1 and gave up 5 earned runs on 5 hits and 2 walks. Detroit got 3 in the 5th and 2 more in the 7th off him. The piece did say that 15 innings is a small sample and treating it as destiny would be the same mistake the rest of the piece was arguing against, so I'll take that one, but let's be honest about what happened: the projection was that Bibee was a problem, and he wasn't.

The stated fear showed up and it didn't matter

From the entry, in the section arguing against my own pick: Cleveland's offense is 28th in baseball at 3.98 runs a game, and against Detroit specifically they've scored 4.00. The one pillar holding up the call had produced nothing in 6 meetings.

Cleveland scored 4. Right on the number, again. They got 1 in the 3rd, then 1 in the 7th, 1 in the 8th and 1 in the 9th chipping at it.

It didn't matter because Detroit scored 6, which is the part the entry got wrong in the direction that helps. Detroit had scored 11 runs in 6 games against Cleveland coming in, 1.83 a game. They got 6 in one night.

One number that moved

Detroit led 6-2 after 7 innings and held it. Yesterday's piece counted 57 leads after 7 this season with 11 lost, so that's 58 and 11. Kyle Finnegan gave up a run in the 8th and Kenley Jansen gave one back in the 9th, and it was a 2 run game with the tying run somewhere in the building, which is about as close to the pattern as you can get without it actually happening.

Javier Báez scored in the 7th on a caught stealing that José Ramírez dropped at third base. That's worth flagging because it's the whole subject of today's other entry, and it's the sort of run this team hasn't been manufacturing.

entry.title: The Wings got handed the hardest schedule in hockey, and it barely matters
entry.summary: Detroit plays 45 games against last season's playoff teams, tied for most in the NHL. Then you look at the spread and the whole league fits inside 3.5 points of opponent quality. The number that actually should worry you is 92 points on a minus 17 goal differential.
entry.content:
The Wings don't play until October 2, home to the Rangers. But the 2026-27 schedule is out, all 84 games of it, so I pulled the whole thing for all 32 teams and scored it. Nobody writes this piece in August, which is exactly why it's worth writing.

First thing worth knowing: it's 84 games now, not 82. That's what the league's own schedule feed says for every team.

The headline, which I don't really believe

Detroit plays 45 games against teams that made the 2026 playoffs. That's the most in the NHL. League average is 42.

Sounds brutal. Then you look at who else is on 45, and it's Florida and Toronto, and suddenly it isn't a curse, it's an address. Those are the 3 Atlantic teams that missed the playoffs last year, and the Atlantic sent 5 of its 8 to the postseason. Buffalo, Tampa, Montreal, Boston, Ottawa. You play each of your division 4 times, so that's 20 of your 45 before anybody sits down to make a schedule.

The formula does the rest. 4 games against each of the 7 division rivals, 3 against each of the 8 in the Metro, 2 against each of the 16 out west. 28 plus 24 plus 32 is 84. There's almost no room in there for the league to do anything to you.

Here's what that looks like when you put every team on the same axis. Average points their opponents earned last season, weighted by how often they meet:

Average opponent points
Toronto, hardest93.89
NY Rangers93.67
Florida93.61
Detroit, 4th93.23
League average92.19
Edmonton90.75
Vegas90.65
Colorado, easiest90.43

Toughest schedule in the league to easiest is 3.5 points of opponent quality. Detroit sits about 1 point above average. Over 84 games that's real but it's not the story, and if the Wings miss by 2 points in April I don't think you get to point at this.

The number in their favour is bigger than the one against

This is the part I didn't expect. Detroit travels 35,625 miles next season, counting great circle distance between arenas and the trips home at each end. That's 4th least in the league. Only Pittsburgh, Buffalo and Philly move less.

League average is 42,464. Seattle does 51,973.

So the Wings will be about 6,800 miles fresher than a typical team and roughly 16,000 fresher than Seattle. In a sport where the whole conversation in March is about legs, that's a bigger edge than 1 point of opponent quality is a disadvantage.

The rest of the fatigue picture is unremarkable. 12 back-to-backs, which is right in the middle, and only 2 of those are the bad kind where they're on the second night and the other team's had at least 2 days off. Longest road trip is 5, longest homestand is 4. 42 home, 42 away.

What should actually worry you

92 points last season. 41-31-10. And a goal differential of minus 17.

Those don't normally go together. Fit points against goal differential across all 32 teams and the line is tight, 91% of the variation, typical miss under 4 points. Detroit finished 5.0 points above what its goals said it should have, 3rd most in the league behind San Jose and Montreal.

Now the honest version of that, because 3rd of 32 sounds worse than it is: the typical team misses the line by 3.9 points, so 5.0 is barely outside ordinary. It's not a scandal. It's a nudge.

But it's a nudge in the wrong direction, and the gap is what makes it sting. The last Eastern wild card was Ottawa at 99. Detroit had 92. That's 7 points short, and if you think even a few of those 92 were borrowed, the real climb is closer to 10 or 12.

You don't get 12 points out of a friendly travel map. You get it from scoring more than you give up, and 241 for and 258 against is a team that didn't.

The thing hanging over all of it

I can't write about the Wings today and skip this. Yzerman's moving to a senior advisor role and there's an actual GM search running, with an outside firm doing it and Shawn Horcoff handling the day to day in the meantime. Reporting says they're prioritizing somebody with a heavy analytics background and might not decide until September.

Which is a little funny given everything above. The next guy is being hired partly to know the difference between a number that means something and a number that just looks scary, and the schedule is about to hand him a great example of the second kind. 45 games against playoff teams is going to get quoted all season. Minus 17 is the one that decides anything.

I'd hold off on reading much into the schedule until we know who's reading it.

What I'll be watching

Goal differential through American Thanksgiving. Not points, not the standings, not whatever a hot October does to everyone's mood. If they're plus by then, the schedule stuff above is noise and this is a playoff team. If they're 12-8-3 with a minus 6, that's last season again and the travel savings won't cover it.

I'll take the under on the schedule being the reason, either way.

Everything above comes from the NHL's public API: the 2026-27 schedule for all 32 clubs and the final 2025-26 standings. The script that derives every number here, including the chart, is scripts/nhl_schedule.py in the repository. Arena coordinates were entered by hand because the league doesn't publish them, and travel is great circle miles between arenas, which isn't the same as flight miles.

entry.title: Somebody said the whole season is the blown saves. So I counted the leads instead.
entry.summary: Detroit has led after 7 innings 57 times and lost 11 of those games. The league holds 90.2% of those leads. At that rate the Tigers would have about 5 more wins, which puts them in first place. The claim checks out.
entry.content:
Somebody on the Tigers sub put it about as plainly as it can be put: the whole season is that blown save number, and if it was 20 instead of 26 we'd be in first. 25 people upvoted it. So I went and checked whether that's actually true.

Here's the thing about blown saves though. A blown save isn't a loss. You can blow 1 in the 8th and win in the 10th, and that still goes in the column. So counting them doesn't tell you what it cost. What tells you is the leads that turned into losses.

So I pulled every inning of every game for all 30 teams and rebuilt the score after 7.

Detroit has led after 7 innings 57 times this year and lost 11 of them.

What everyone else does with a lead

The league held 1,436 of 1,592 leads after 7. That's 90.2%.

Every completed game through Aug 10, rebuilt from the linescores on the MLB Stats API. Script's in the repo, run it yourself.

Tampa's led after 7 60 times and lost 1. Detroit's had 3 fewer chances and lost 11.

What it cost, in wins

At the league rate Detroit loses about 5.6 of those 57 leads. They lost 11. So call it 5 extra losses, and those 5 are the whole argument.

58-60 becomes roughly 63-55. Chicago's at 61-56. That's first place, by about a game and a half, and it's the middle of August.

So yeah, the guy was right.

Where I'd push back on myself

A couple of things before anybody takes 63-55 as gospel.

Not every one of those 11 was a save situation. Detroit was up 5-1 after 7 on March 31 and lost 7-5, and that's a starter and a middle reliever coming apart, not a closer. The blown save number and the lost lead number overlap a lot but they aren't the same list.

And you don't automatically win the ones you don't lose. Some of those games are tied in the 9th and you're playing extras either way. The 5 wins is the ceiling of the argument, not a promise.

There's also a thing that cuts the other direction and nobody mentions it. Detroit has led after 7 in 57 games, which is 7th most in baseball. They keep getting into these positions. The bullpen is what it is, but the rest of the team keeps handing it leads to lose, and a team that couldn't get there wouldn't even have the complaint.

The narrower version

Leads after 8 are the closer's problem more cleanly. Detroit's led after 8 in 54 games and lost 5. That's better. It's still 5.

Tonight it's Bibee against Anderson, and 5 of the 6 games against Cleveland this year came down to 1 or 2 runs. If this series turns on a 1 run game in the 8th, now you know what the number behind that feeling actually is.

entry.title: Pick No. 3: Detroit released this pitcher in April 2024. Tuesday he starts against the team standing between them and October
entry.summary: Drew Anderson was let go by the Toledo Mud Hens two years ago, spent four years in Japan and Korea, and is now the Tigers' answer to trading Tarik Skubal. He has never faced more than 18 batters in a major league game. He gets Tanner Bibee, who has a 1.80 ERA against Detroit this year, in a game Detroit has to have.
entry.content:
The call: Tigers beat Cleveland on Tuesday night at Comerica. Confidence: low. Detroit is 0-6 against this team, and the man they are handing the ball to was released by their own Triple-A club twenty-seven months ago.

Start with that, because it is the most Detroit sentence available. On April 27, 2024, the Toledo Mud Hens released a 30-year-old right-hander named Drew Anderson. Tuesday night, in a game the Tigers cannot really afford to lose, he takes the mound at Comerica Park against the best starter Cleveland has.

The four years in between

Anderson signed with Philadelphia in 2012, a kid out of Reno. He gave the Phillies seven years, most of them injured, and 21 major league innings with a 7.71 ERA. They released him in September 2019. The White Sox signed him, used him for one and a third innings in 2020, and released him too. That winter he pitched for the Melbourne Aces in the Australian Baseball League. Texas gave him 22 innings in 2021 and released him in October.

Then he left. Two years with the Hiroshima Toyo Carp in Japan. A spring training invite from Detroit in 2024 that ended with Toledo cutting him in April. And then the part that matters: two seasons with the SSG Landers in Korea, where in 2025 he went 12-7 with a 2.27 ERA and 245 strikeouts in 171 and two thirds innings. That is not a guy hanging on. That is one of the best pitchers in a good league.

Detroit signed him back in December, one year, seven million dollars, with a ten million dollar club option for 2027. He is 32.

What he has actually done here

The Tigers used him as a long reliever for four months and he was good at it: 41 appearances, 67 and a third innings, a 4.01 ERA, 78 strikeouts against 25 walks. That is a 27 percent strikeout rate, which is genuinely excellent, and an 8.7 percent walk rate, which is not.

Then the deadline happened. Detroit traded Tarik Skubal and Casey Mize, which is a sentence that still looks strange in print, and on August 4 A.J. Hinch announced that Anderson and Jackson Jobe were being stretched out as starters. Anderson made his first one the next day.

So the rotation that is supposed to carry a wild card push includes a converted long man making his fourth start and a kid coming back from Tommy John surgery.

The number that decides Tuesday

Here is the honest problem, and it is not about how good Anderson is.

He has never faced more than 18 batters in a major league game. Not this year, not ever. Eighteen was his ceiling on May 20, and he needed 63 pitches to get there.

Anderson's three startsLineBatters facedPitches

One earned run in eleven innings across the three. The stuff is not the question. The question is the third column.

A Detroit start this season has faced a median of 22 batters. Nineteen of the team's 118 starts have ended at 18 batters or fewer, and five of those ended at five batters or fewer, which is a bullpen game wearing a starter's name. Anderson's best day is still below the middle of that distribution.

Which means the bullpen covers four innings, maybe five, against a division rival. That same bullpen has 23 saves and 26 blown saves, a 47 percent conversion rate, second worst in baseball, behind a 3.49 team ERA that says the arms are fine and the sequencing is not. On Sunday in San Francisco it blew another one in the seventh and Detroit won in the tenth anyway. That is not a plan, that is a coin landing correctly.

So why am I taking the Tigers

Because of one number that everybody covering this series is going to skip.

Cleveland's offense is 28th in baseball. Not bad, not slumping: 28th of 30, 3.97 runs a game. Detroit scores 4.57 and sits 11th. Detroit's run differential is plus 87. Cleveland's is minus 27. That is a 114-run gap between two teams a single game apart in the standings, and the standings are the thing that is lying, not the run differential.

Cleveland has lost seven of ten. Detroit has won seven of ten and is a game out of the last wild card spot. Detroit is 30-27 at home. And the six-game sweep that everyone will lead with, I already went and tested: hold every team's game-by-game run totals fixed, shuffle which opponent they came against, two thousand times, and 74 percent of those shuffled seasons produce a worst matchup at least as extreme as Detroit's against Cleveland. It is the worst offensive split in baseball and it is still the kind of thing chance hands out most years to somebody.

That test ran yesterday, on this same series, and it said the sweep is the kind of thing chance produces. Picking Cleveland tonight would mean deciding that a finding published one day ago stops applying the moment it is inconvenient.

What scares me

The best argument against everything above, and I did not see it until I went looking for it. The 28th-ranked offense line is doing a lot of work in this entry, so here is what that offense has actually done to Detroit: 24 runs in six games, 4.00 a game, against a season rate of 3.97. Cleveland has not been a bad offense against the Tigers. They have been exactly themselves, and they have won every time, because Detroit scored 1.83. The gap in this series has been entirely on Detroit's side of the ball. So the pillar I am leaning on, that a weak lineup will not hurt Anderson, is the one pillar that has produced nothing at all in six tries.

Tanner Bibee, next. He has made two starts against Detroit this year and thrown 15 innings with three earned runs, a 1.80 ERA, and Detroit put four hits on him in eight innings on May 20. The rest of the league has done better: 3.85 for the season, and 23 home runs allowed in 138 innings, which is 1.50 per nine and the one seam in him. Detroit has to find it, at home, off a guy who has not given them anything all year.

Third, the shape of the May 20 game is the exact nightmare. Anderson threw four and two thirds shutout innings with seven strikeouts against this same lineup, Bibee threw eight, and Cleveland won 3-2. Detroit's starter being excellent has already failed to be enough once in this precise matchup, with these two pitchers, in this ballpark, eighty-three days ago.

The call

Better team, at home, with the better lineup, against the third worst offense in baseball, riding a converted reliever who has been terrific in a role he has never held for more than 63 pitches. If Anderson gives them four and the bullpen does not do the thing it does half the time, Detroit wins.

That is a lot of ifs, which is exactly what Low means.

Tigers win. Low confidence.

entry.title: The Tigers are 0-6 against Cleveland with the worst offensive matchup in baseball. I went looking for the reason and found out there probably isn't one
entry.summary: Detroit has scored 11 runs in six games against the Guardians, 1.83 a game against a season average of 4.58. Out of 294 team-opponent pairs in baseball, that is the single worst. Then I shuffled who played whom two thousand times, and pure chance produced a worst matchup more extreme than Detroit's in 74 percent of the shuffles. The tell is that the same Tigers own the other tail too.
entry.content:
Cleveland comes to Comerica on Tuesday and the Tigers have not beaten them all year. Not once. Six games, six losses, and the losses were not the fun kind where you get blown out and forget about it by Thursday. Four of the six were decided by one or two runs.

This is the one thing about Detroit's season that the regression argument does not touch. I wrote last week that Detroit's close-game record is about 61 percent as meaningful as it looks, which covers a lot of ground, and a reader correctly pointed out that it does not cover this. You can tell me that 26-44 in close games will regress. Fine. Tell me about 0-6 against the one team sitting directly between Detroit and a wild card, with seven more games left against them.

So I went and looked at all six games, and then at every other team-opponent matchup in baseball, and the answer is genuinely not what I expected when I started.

First, how bad it actually is

Every completed Detroit-Cleveland game in 2026, matched by the league's own game id. The June 14 game was postponed and is on the September 4 schedule as a makeup, which is why it is not a seventh loss here.

Eleven runs in six games. That is 1.83 a game from a team that scores 4.58 for the season. Detroit struck out in 30.6 percent of its at-bats in these six games against a season rate of 25.6 percent, and left 92 men on base.

Cleveland scored 24, and 8 of those came in the first game. Take out the opener and it is Cleveland 16, Detroit 9 across five games. Nobody was hitting. Detroit was hitting less.

It is not the bullpen, and I want to be clear about that because it is the easy answer

The Tigers' bullpen is the story of this season. Twenty-two saves and 25 blown ones. It is the reason the record does not match the run differential, and if you had asked me to guess why Detroit is 0-6 against Cleveland before I pulled the game logs, that is what I would have guessed.

It is wrong.

Detroit's relievers threw 24 innings in this series with a 3.38 ERA, and four of those nine earned runs came in one third of an inning from Brant Hurter in the May 18 blowout. Take that one appearance out and the bullpen ran a 2.25 across the rest of it. That is not a unit that lost six games.

Here is the number that settles it: in these six games, Detroit led at the end of an inning from the sixth onward exactly once. You cannot blow a lead you never had. The bullpen was not handing these back. The offense never gave them anything to hand back.

What did happen is that Cleveland's relievers threw 17 innings and gave up one earned run. Cade Smith appeared in four of the six. Tanner Bibee started two of them and went 15 innings with three earned runs, and he is the probable starter on Tuesday.

So is this a real thing about the matchup?

Here is where I expected to write a paragraph about how Detroit's lineup has some specific problem with Cleveland's staff, and instead I have to write this.

Minus 2.75 runs per game is a huge number. Out of every team-opponent pair in baseball with at least six games played, 294 of them, Detroit against Cleveland is the single worst offensive matchup in the sport. Rank one of 294.

The problem with that sentence is that somebody has to be rank one of 294. The real question is not whether minus 2.75 is a big number. It is whether minus 2.75 is bigger than the worst number 294 coin flips produce.

So I tested it. Hold every team's actual game-by-game runs scored exactly as they happened, then shuffle which of those games belong to which opponent, keeping the number of games in each matchup the same. Recompute all 294 splits. Write down the worst one. Do that two thousand times, and you have a picture of what the most extreme matchup in baseball looks like when opponent identity means literally nothing.

The result:

  • Detroit-Cleveland, observed: minus 2.75 runs per game.
  • The worst pair in a shuffled season, median outcome: minus 2.94.
  • Shuffles that produced a worst matchup at least as extreme as Detroit's: 1,473 of 2,000, or 73.7 percent.

The most alarming number in the Tigers' season is milder than what pure randomness typically hands you. In a league where nobody has any matchup problems with anybody, the worst-looking pair is usually worse than this one.

The part that convinced me

I could have stopped there and some of you would reasonably say the simulation is a trick. Here is the thing that is not a trick.

Detroit is rank 1 of 294 in the worst direction. Detroit is also rank 292 of 294 in the best direction, scoring 8.00 runs a game against the Athletics, plus 3.42 over their season rate, in a 6-0 sweep. And while doing it, Detroit held those same Athletics to 1.83 runs a game, which is the fifth most extreme offensive suppression in baseball.

Same team. Same season. Both tails of the distribution, plus a third entry near the end. If Detroit having the worst offensive matchup in baseball proves something is broken about how they match up with Cleveland, then Detroit having nearly the best proves they have solved the Athletics forever, and Tigers fans who watched this team for four months know exactly how much that is worth.

Two more things in the same direction. Seven team-opponent pairs in baseball are winless at six or more games, including the Mets at 0-7 against the Cubs and the Padres at 0-6 against Philadelphia. If you work out how many sweeps you would expect from team strength alone, using each club's season win rate, the answer is 5.0. Seven observed against five expected is not a phenomenon. And Cleveland is not some offense-eating machine: the second-worst matchup in baseball is Cleveland scoring 1.33 a game against Tampa Bay.

What I would still watch on Tuesday

None of the above means 0-6 was fake. Those are six real losses in the standings and Detroit is 57-60, two games back of a wild card, with Cleveland at 58-60 sitting a half game in front of them. The games happened. The argument is only about what they predict.

The one thing that survives every test above is that Tanner Bibee has thrown 15 innings against Detroit this year and given up three earned runs, and he takes the ball Tuesday at 6:40. That is not a statistical artifact of a small sample the way the team-level split is, it is one pitcher who has had a specific plan and executed it twice. It is also, and I have to say this because it is the same trap, fifteen innings. Two starts. If I told you a pitcher was now permanently good against a lineup on the strength of two starts I would be doing exactly the thing this piece just spent a thousand words arguing against.

So: I am not scared of the 0-6. I am mildly scared of Bibee, and mostly I want to see whether a Detroit lineup that struck out in 30.6 percent of its at-bats against this staff can hand its bullpen a lead late. Across six games it has done that once.

The pick for Tuesday's game goes up before first pitch, as always, on the record page. This piece is not it. This piece is me finding out that the scariest thing on Detroit's schedule is a coin that came up tails six times.

Method and sources: all game data from the MLB Stats API, regular season only, matched by gamePk and filtered on abstractGameState rather than the detailed status string, which reports real completed games as "Game Over" and "Completed Early." Series detail from scripts/det_cle_series.py, the distribution and permutation test from scripts/opponent_splits.py, the chart from scripts/opponent_split_chart.py, all in the repository. The permutation test uses a fixed seed so anyone can reproduce the 73.7 percent exactly.

Not betting advice. Just calls, made in public and kept in public.

entry.title: The Pistons just made the biggest two-year climb in the NBA since 1993. I went looking for the crash that is supposed to follow it
entry.summary: Detroit went 14-68, then 44-38, then 60-22. That is a gain of 46 wins in two seasons and nothing in thirty-four years of standings matches it. The fear is that a climb that steep has to come back down. Fifteen teams have climbed anything like it, and what they did next runs both ways with no signal in it. What does predict next season is duller: Detroit is a 60-win team now, and 60-win teams give back about five.
entry.content:
Three summers ago the Pistons lost 68 games. This spring they won 60, finished first in the Eastern Conference, and got run out of their own building 125-94 in a Game 7 they hosted. Then the offseason: Jalen Duren's restricted free agency stalled, Detroit's search for a second scorer alongside Cade Cunningham ended with no deal, and four rotation players left in Tobias Harris, Isaiah Stewart, Caris LeVert and Marcus Sasser.

So the worry going around is specific, and it is not stupid. Teams that rise that fast are supposed to fall. The roster that won 60 is not quite the roster coming back. The East got harder.

The first half of that is the part people assert instead of checking, so I pulled every NBA season since 1991 and went looking for teams who climbed the way Detroit climbed.

There is no team who climbed the way Detroit climbed

Detroit went from 14 wins to 44 to 60. Out of 995 other three-season spans in the sample, the number that gained as much as Detroit's 46 is zero. The closest is Philadelphia in 2018, at 42.

TeamSeasonFromToGainNext year
Detroit Pistons20261460+46not played

Miami Heat20101547+32+11
Oklahoma City Thunder20112355+32+3

Two things about that table that change how you should read it.

Four seasons in this window were not 82 games: the 1999 lockout, 2012, and the two covid years. Everything here is converted to a wins-per-82 pace, marked with a dot. That conversion is necessary in one direction and misleading in the other. It stops a 50-game season from looking like a collapse, but it also manufactures climbs nobody watched. San Antonio's 1999 row reads as a 61-win team and they won 37 games, in a 50-game season, and their "-8" the next year was really 37 wins becoming 53. Phoenix in 2021 won 51, not 58. Read the dotted rows as rates, not as seasons that happened.

The other thing is the three-way tie at +32. All three are in the table because cutting the list at a round number would have dropped two teams who got better the next year and kept the one who got worse, which would have made the right column look like something it is not.

What those teams did next

Take the fifteen teams with a climb of 30 wins or more that have a following season on record. Their median change the next year was minus 1.0 wins. Now take every season in the sample at a pace of 58 wins or better: median change minus 6.0, with 69 of 83 declining.

On those two numbers the big leapers look better than ordinary very good teams. That comparison is worthless, and the table above shows why. The leapers' peaks run from 43 wins to 66, with a median of 53. A 53-win team regresses less than a 62-win team for a reason that has nothing to do with how either of them got there: there is less above it to fall from. Comparing a group of mostly-53-win teams against a group of all-60-plus-win teams measures the difference in their peaks, not the difference in their histories.

So match them. For each of the fifteen leapers, take every non-leaping team-season whose win pace was within three wins of that leaper's, and ask what those teams did the following year. That is the number the leaper has to beat.

TeamSeasonPeakActual next yearMatched teamsDifference

Phoenix Suns202158+6-5.0+10.9

Miami Heat200559-7-5.0-2.0

Oklahoma City Thunder201050+5-2.2+7.2
Houston Rockets2025520-2.7+2.7

Median difference: plus 2.7 wins. Nine of fifteen beat their matched group.

Nine of fifteen is what a coin produces; the odds of nine or more heads in fifteen flips are about three in ten. Resample those fifteen differences twenty thousand times and the middle 95 percent of the median runs from minus 2.0 to plus 7.2 wins, an interval with zero sitting inside it. Drop every span that touches a shortened season and ten cases remain, median plus 2.8, seven of ten positive, which is the same non-answer.

The two largest positives are Miami in 2010, who added LeBron James and Chris Bosh, and Oklahoma City in 2024, a very young team that kept improving. Those are not evidence that leaping helps. They are evidence that what happens to the roster in July matters, which everyone already knew.

So the crash is not a thing the record shows. The careful version of that sentence matters, because with fifteen cases spread from minus 11 to plus 14, this design cannot see an effect smaller than about five wins in either direction. It rules out the big scary version. It does not prove the climb is meaningless.

Two more holes worth naming. The matched pool is non-leaping teams at the same win level, which by construction means teams that arrived there flat or falling, and a team that dropped to 52 from 58 is not the same animal as one that rose to 52 from 45. And the fifteen differences are not independent, because leapers with similar peaks share most of their control seasons, so that bootstrap interval is a little narrower than it should be. Cutting the other way: selecting teams on a huge positive swing partly selects on a lucky peak season, which should drag the leapers' next-year numbers down. That bias runs against the leapers and they still came out even.

What does carry information

One thing, and it is unglamorous. Detroit is a 60-win team now, and that is itself the prediction.

Of the 86 team-seasons in the sample that finished within three wins of a 60-win pace, the median lost 5.2 wins the following year. 62 of the 86 declined at all. 24 of the 86, better than one in four, fell below 50 wins.

That is the base rate and it applies to Detroit exactly as it applied to everyone else. It is also milder than the mood suggests. Five wins off 60 is 55 wins. The scenario Pistons fans are bracing for is not the median outcome, it is the one-in-four outcome, and one in four is a real risk rather than a prophecy.

The call

Detroit finishes next season between 52 and 58 wins. That is the number that gets graded, and it is deliberately narrow enough to be wrong: the base rate alone would let me say "fewer than 60" and be right 62 times out of 86, which is not a call, it is a hedge.

The limit on all of this is roster continuity, and I did not measure it. Every number above treats a team as a win total, so it cannot tell a 60-win team bringing everyone back from a 60-win team that lost four rotation players and has an All-NBA center whose contract is unsettled. Duren is still listed on Detroit's roster today. If that changes, none of these base rates knew about it.

That is the thing worth watching this fall. It was never the 46.

Standings from ESPN's public API, every season from 1991 through 2026, pulled and analysed by scripts/nba_leaps.py; the chart comes from the same run via scripts/nba_leap_chart.py. Franchise spans are joined across relocations, so Seattle to Oklahoma City counts as one team. Offseason reporting via PistonPowered and Sports Illustrated; Game 7 via ESPN. Not betting advice.

entry.title: Graded: Pick No. 2, Tigers at Giants. Correct in ten innings, and wrong about both pitchers
entry.summary: The call was Tigers win, Low confidence. Final: Detroit 3, San Francisco 1 in ten. The pick landed and the two arguments holding it up both fell over inside the first seven innings.
entry.content:
The call, committed before first pitch: Tigers win. Confidence Low.

The result: Detroit 3, San Francisco 1, ten innings. gamePk 823190, confirmed Final against the MLB Stats API.

Record: 2-0.

Now the part worth reading, which is that almost none of the reasoning survived the game.

Melton did not regress

Half of Sunday's entry was an argument that Troy Melton's 1.58 ERA was built on a .191 batting average on balls in play, the lowest of 141 qualifying starters in baseball, and that the correction could land on any given Sunday including that one.

It did not land. Six innings, four hits, one walk, five strikeouts, no earned runs, 92 pitches. His ERA went down, to 1.46 over 80 innings.

The one honest thing to pull out of the line: balls put in play against him Sunday fell in at .250, sixteen balls in play and four hits. That is well above his season rate and still under the .287 league median for a starter. So the day was a small step toward the thing I predicted and nowhere near the correction I described. Sixteen balls in play settles nothing, which is exactly what the original piece said about small samples and is worth applying to the sample that flattered me too.

Webb was excellent

The other leg of the pick was that Logan Webb had a 5.45 ERA across his last six starts and a 6.59 in July, and that this was the version of him Detroit would meet.

He threw eight innings and gave up one run on four hits and a walk, with twelve ground outs. Whatever the last six starts said about him did not show up. San Francisco lost that game anyway, which is its own kind of brutal.

So the pick was right on the teams and wrong on both starters. Detroit is a better club than San Francisco by run differential, by offense, by roughly every measure the entry cited, and that is the leg that carried it. The pitching matchup, which is what the piece actually spent its words on, went to the Giants and did not matter.

The bullpen did exactly what I said it would

This is the part I want on the record, because it is the first time the stated fear actually arrived.

From Sunday's entry: "Detroit has 22 saves and 25 blown saves in 47 opportunities. Forty seven percent. The team ERA is 3.55, which is good, and the bullpen keeps handing back leads anyway."

Melton left in the seventh with a 1-0 lead, a runner on first and nobody out. Kyle Finnegan came in. A force out, then a Drew Gilbert single, and the game was tied. That is Detroit's 26th blown save in 49 chances, 47 percent, right on the season rate. Eight of the 26 belong to Finnegan.

What is different is what happened next. Drew Sommers, Kenley Jansen and Tyler Holton threw three and a third innings without allowing a base runner between them, striking out seven. Then Hao-Yu Lee singled in the tenth to score Riley Greene, and Max Clark forced in a second run, and Holton struck out the side in the bottom half.

Detroit blew the lead and won anyway. That is not the shape of the ten-win gap; it is the opposite of it.

One number that moved

Detroit is now 27-44 in games decided by three runs or fewer, and 31-16 in games decided by four or more. Sunday was a two-run game, so it goes in the bucket this team has spent all season losing.

The close-game piece from earlier this week argued that Detroit's .371 in those games regresses toward about .442 over the rest of the schedule, worth roughly two wins. One game proves nothing about that. It is one game in the right direction, and there are 44 left to see whether the rest follow.

The Tigers sit 58-60, three and a half back of the White Sox in the Central and one game out of the last wild card with Cleveland arriving at Comerica Tuesday.

Sources: MLB Stats API, pulled 2026-08-09, for the final, the box score, the play by play, both pitching lines, team save and blown save totals, the close game splits computed from Detroit's own game log, and the standings.

Not betting advice. Just calls, made in public and kept in public.

entry.title: Graded: Pick No. 1, Tigers at Giants. Correct, 8-0, and the reasoning was only half right
entry.summary: The call was Tigers win, Low confidence. Final: Tigers 8, Giants 0. Record moves to 1-0. The pick was right and one of the two things it leaned on did not happen at all.
entry.content:
The call, committed before first pitch: Tigers win. Confidence Low.

The result: Detroit 8, San Francisco 0. Nine innings, gamePk 823188, confirmed Final against the MLB Stats API.

Record: 1-0.

A win is a win and I will take it. But a graded note that only says "correct" is worth nothing, so here is the part that did not go according to the argument.

The pick leaned on two things. The first was that Detroit is a far better team than its record, which is why the run differential piece existed in the first place. That held up completely. An 8-0 road shutout is the version of this team the underlying numbers keep insisting is real.

The second was the bullpen, and specifically the worry that Detroit's problem is never getting a lead but keeping one. That was never tested. The game was 8-0. Nobody warmed up in a save situation, nothing was handed back after the seventh, and the single most likely way for this pick to lose never got a chance to happen. I called it Low precisely because of that risk, and then the risk sat out the game.

That matters for how much credit the call deserves, which is: some, not a lot. Detroit is 31-16 in games decided by four or more and 26-44 in games decided by three or fewer. This one landed in the first bucket by the third inning. The pick was correct and it was correct in the easy way.

Low was the right label. A better team beating a worse team is a coin flip with a thumb on it, and the thumb showed up. If every one of these came in at 8-0 the confidence labels on this board would be decoration.

One down, and the full record is on the homepage, win or lose, permanently.

Not betting advice. Just calls, made in public and kept in public.

entry.title: Are the Tigers bad at close games, or unlucky? Five seasons say both, and mostly the second one
entry.summary: Readers pushed back on the regression argument: losing close games might be who this team is, not luck waiting to reverse. That is testable. Across 150 team-seasons, a close-game record carries about 61 percent of the repeatable signal an ordinary stretch of schedule carries. Not zero, and not close to all of it. For Detroit it is worth about two wins over the last 45 games, and the reader objection that actually survives is a different one.
entry.content:
Last week I wrote that the Tigers were the best team in the AL Central and in fourth place, and that the gap between their record and their run differential was a promise the rest of the season would keep.

The comments on that piece were better than the piece. The sharpest one said the reasoning was not just optimistic but conceptually wrong: run differential and Pythagorean expectation get read as a guarantee of regression, and they are not. Blowing out the Athletics does not put a run in the bank. A team that keeps losing one-run games might simply be a team that is bad at one-run games, and calling that luck is just refusing to look at it.

That is a real argument and I did not test it before publishing. So here it is, tested, with the answer up front: the reader is right about the mechanism and wrong about the size. Close-game performance is partly a real, repeatable property of a team. It is roughly 61 percent as repeatable as an equal number of ordinary games. That leaves Detroit better than its close-game record but worse than the pure-regression story implies, and it moves the projection by about two wins rather than the seven the Pythagorean gap advertises.

What Detroit's season actually looks like split by margin

SplitRecordWin rate
Overall57-60.487
Decided by 3 runs or fewer26-44.371
One-run games12-20.375
Decided by 4 or more31-16.660
vs AL Central11-18.379

Every game Detroit has played through the final whistle on August 8, from the MLB Stats API, regular season only.

A reader also corrected the framing I used, and the correction was an improvement. I had leaned on the 12-20 one-run split. The better number is 26-44 in games decided by three or fewer: same story, 70 games instead of 32. Their figure was 26-45 and the true one is 26-44, off by a single loss, which is closer than most published numbers get.

That 31-16 in blowouts is the part nobody talks about. Detroit beats good teams badly and loses to bad teams narrowly, and the distance between those two things is not normal.

Detroit is not merely at the top of that list. At +.288 the gap is more than 1.6 times the second-place Cubs at +.173, and the gap between Detroit and the Cubs is wider than the gap between the Cubs and ninth place. Whatever is happening here, it is happening to the Tigers more than to anyone else in baseball.

TeamBlowout win rateClose-game win rateGap
Tigers.660 (31-16).371 (26-44)+.288
Cubs.673 (35-17).500 (33-33)+.173
Pirates.564 (31-24).422 (27-37)+.142
Brewers.702 (33-14).571 (40-30)+.131
Braves.660 (31-16).549 (39-32)+.110
...
Astros.378 (17-28).589 (43-30)-.211

The number I found first, and why I am not using it

There is an obvious explanation sitting right there. Detroit has converted 22 of 47 save opportunities, 47 percent, with 25 blown saves, second most in baseball, behind a pitching staff whose 3.52 team ERA is fourth best in all of MLB. Good pitching, handed back after the seventh.

Across the 30 teams, save conversion rate correlates with close-game win rate at r = +.783, and with blowout win rate at +.069. That looks like a smoking gun: bullpen quality drives close games and nothing else.

It is not evidence, and I want to be the one to say so. A save opportunity is by definition a lead of three runs or fewer, and a blown save in a close game very often is the close loss. The two statistics are built out of overlapping events. Correlating them measures the dictionary, not the world. If I published that +.783 as proof, someone would eventually notice, and they would be right.

So the test has to be one where the answer is not baked in.

The actual test

If losing close games is a property of a team, then a team's close games should predict its own other close games. Deal each team's close games alternately into two piles, odd and even, and correlate the win rate in one pile against the other across every team. Same roster, same manager, same bullpen, no aging, no trades in between. That is the friendliest possible test of the skill hypothesis. Then run the identical test on all games as a control, because team quality is unquestionably real and has to survive it.

On the 2026 season alone, it does not settle anything:

Split-half test, 2026 onlyr
All games+.432
Games decided by 3 or fewer+.093
All games, thinned to the same sample size+.211
Literal coin flips, same sample sizes.000 (90 percent of simulations land between -.312 and +.304)

Thirty teams is not enough. The coin-flip simulation shows that a correlation anywhere inside roughly plus or minus .30 is what pure randomness produces at these sample sizes, and both the close-game figure and its control sit inside that band. Anyone who stopped here and reported "+.097, therefore luck" would be reporting noise with a decimal point on it.

So I ran the same thing over the five completed seasons from 2021 through 2025, which gives 150 team-seasons instead of 30, on full schedules instead of two-thirds of one:

Split-half test, 150 team-seasonsr
All games+.640
Games decided by 3 or fewer+.290
All games, thinned to the same sample size+.583

Now it separates cleanly, and the comparison that matters is the last two rows, because they use identical sample sizes. A random slice of a team's schedule predicts the rest of that team's schedule at +.583. The same number of close games predicts the team's other close games at +.290.

Stepping those up to full-season reliability gives .449 for close games against .737 for ordinary ones. A close-game record carries about 61 percent of the repeatable signal that the same number of ordinary games carries.

That is the answer to the objection, and it is a split decision. Close-game performance is not noise. Something real and repeatable is in there, and a reader who says "this team is bad at close games" is describing something that exists. But it is a good deal less real than the raw record makes it look, and treating 26-44 as a fixed property of the Tigers overstates it by a wide margin.

What that is worth, in wins

Regressing Detroit's .371 by that reliability puts their true close-game talent at about .442. Sixty percent of their games this year have been decided by three or fewer, so call it 27 close games in the 45 that remain.

Record in the next 27 close games
At their observed .37110.0-17.0
At the regressed .44211.9-15.1
Differenceabout +1.9 wins

Two wins. Not the seven that the Pythagorean gap dangles, and not zero either. Detroit is 2.0 games back of the third wild card. Two wins is the whole difference between playing in October and watching, which is a genuinely strange place for an argument about statistical reliability to land.

For what it is worth on the luck side of the ledger: if close games were coin flips, a team playing 70 of them finishes 26-44 or worse about 2.1 percent of the time. That is unusual. It is also the kind of unusual that shows up somewhere every year when 30 teams each get a turn.

The objection that survives all of this

A different reader made a point that none of the above touches, and it is the best argument against everything I wrote last week.

Detroit's worst split is against its own division: 11-18, a .379 clip. Last week's piece argued that the 20-odd remaining head-to-head games against the teams ahead of them were the path back into the race. Against a team playing .379 ball in exactly those games, the same schedule is the fastest available route to elimination.

Here is what I found looking into it, and it cuts both ways:

Detroit vs AL CentralRecord
Overall11-18
In games decided by 3 or fewer9-14
In blowouts2-4
vs Cleveland0-6
vs Cleveland, games decided by 3 or fewer0-5

The division record is almost entirely a close-game record. Twenty-three of those 29 games were decided by three runs or fewer, which is a far higher share than the 60 percent Detroit runs overall. So the division problem and the close-game problem are not two independent pieces of evidence stacking up against the Tigers. They are largely the same fact counted twice, and the regression above applies to most of it.

But 0-6 against Cleveland, with five of those six decided by three or fewer, is its own small horror. Seven of Detroit's remaining 45 games are against Cleveland, and 23 of the 45 are inside the division. A team that has not beaten the Guardians once all year now needs that specific matchup more than any other on the schedule.

That is the honest state of it. The close-game record is about 61 percent as meaningful as it looks, which is worth roughly two wins and probably a wild card spot. The division record is mostly the same finding wearing a different hat. And a winless record against the team they will see seven more times is not something any correlation coefficient is going to explain away.

One correction, on a number nobody asked about

While pulling this data I found that my own earlier recomputation of Detroit's record gave 55-60 where the standings said 56-60. The missing game is April 4 against St. Louis, an 11-6 Tigers win called for rain. The MLB API returns it with a status of "Completed Early" rather than "Final", and my filter matched only the exact string "Final", so a real win vanished from every game-by-game calculation I ran. It is fixed here and in the backtest script. With Saturday night's 8-0 win in San Francisco added, the Tigers are 57-60.

It is a small thing. It is also exactly the kind of thing that quietly corrupts a number in a piece like this, and the only reason it got caught is that a recomputed figure disagreed with a published one by exactly one game and I wrote it down instead of shrugging.

Sourcing: every game result, margin and standing here comes from the MLB Stats API, pulled 2026-08-09. Season data covers 1,757 decided regular-season games in 2026 through August 8, plus the complete 2021 through 2025 regular seasons for the reliability test. Bullpen figures are the team pitching endpoint for the same date. The chart and every figure in it are generated by scripts/close_gap_chart.py; the reliability tests are scripts/close_games.py, which takes --margin and --seasons so anyone can re-run them at a different definition of "close". Both are in the repository along with this entry.

Not betting advice. Just analysis, made in public and kept in public.

entry.title: Fourth place, best team in the division, and half the schedule left against the teams ahead
entry.summary: The Tigers have the best run differential in the AL Central and the fourth-best record in it. Twenty of their remaining forty-six games are against the three teams they are chasing, which is the most concentrated stretch run in baseball. Here is the case for the comeback, and the three numbers that argue against it.
entry.content:
The AL Central standings this morning read like a joke with no punchline.
